rv.q: How has this English country-house whodunnit lasted?

The world has stayed true to her wish. Audiences leaving the show are implored by the cast to keep the identity of the killer to themselves once they leave the theatre, so we’ll say nothing more, other than that this classic English country house murder mystery is perfect for an evening of traditional, captivating storytelling.

I loved every sympathy- and suspicion-shifting minute of it, with sterling work especially from Alexander Wolfe as the highly strung character of Christopher Wren, one of a slew of hotel guests wriggling under the stern gaze of Paul Hilliar’s no-nonsense Detective Sergeant Trotter.
Abandon yourself to the sheer silliness of it all.
This is a beautifully preserved example of a country house murder mystery, a throwback to theatregoing in the thirties (minus the matinee tea-trays).
The story, whilst sensational and full of silly coincidences, is actually quite good.
The real mystery of the world's longest-running theatre show is not whodunit but, in its currently mediocre state, whydoit at all?
Still looks and feels fresh and could easily run for another seventy
